principles.name: Where The Money Comes From

feedback.correct: n/a — concept rule

principles.rationale: In no-limit hold 'em, money comes from opponents putting money into the pot with bad hands that a perfect player would not play. You exploit this by betting and raising to extract value or force folds.

principles.name: The early-position opening range

feedback.correct: The early-position list is about 14 percent of hands: raise what is on it, fold what is not.
feedback.too_passive: Limping splits your range into identifiable strength buckets.
feedback.too_tight: This hand is on the list. Folding it plays fewer than the 14 percent this seat is built around, and the frequency is the point.
feedback.wrong_sizing: Ten or twelve dollars at 1-2. Raising bigger from early position bloats a pot you will play out of position.
feedback.too_loose: This hand is not on the early-position list, and there are only about 14 hands in a hundred that are. "More than five out of six times you will fold" — playing it out of position is the leak the list exists to close.

principles.rationale: "You also execute a sound pre-flop strategy by consistently raising if no one has raised ahead of you. Raising punishes your opponents for playing too many hands. And it bloats the pot, which increases the size of your opponents' errors later." (p.57) From early position, "if no one has raised in front of you, I recommend you play roughly 14 percent of hands" — all pocket pairs, all suited aces, any two suited cards ten and higher, suited connectors down to 7-6, and ace-king and ace-queen offsuit (p.59). Everything else is folded: "more than five out of six times, you will look at your hand and fold".

feedback.correct: On the early-position list, and the list is raised — "consistently raising if no one has raised ahead of you ... punishes your opponents for playing too many hands" (p.57).

principles.name: The cutoff opening range

feedback.correct: The cutoff list is about 22 percent of hands: raise what is on it, fold what is not.
feedback.too_passive: Limping fails to build a pot.
feedback.too_tight: The cutoff plays 22 percent, not 14. Folding this is playing an early-position range from a late-position seat.

principles.name: The button opening range

feedback.too_passive: Limping surrenders button equity.

principles.name: Raise the good hands in a limped pot (big blind)

feedback.correct: Over limpers in the big blind, raise the good hands and take the free flop with the rest.
feedback.too_passive: Checking in the blinds invites multiway disaster.
feedback.too_aggressive: You already have a free look at the flop from the big blind. Raising a hand off the list builds a pot you will play out of position against everyone who limped in.
feedback.wrong_sizing: "Typically four players limp, and the blinds call and check for a six-way flop. But if someone makes it $15 or $20 after three limpers, only one or two players are likely to call the raise" (pp.76-77). Size the raise to the game in front of you, not to the habit.

principles.rationale: "In limped pots, where one or more players will tend to call a raise, just raise the good hands." (p.68)

feedback.correct: "In limped pots, where one or more players will tend to call a raise, just raise the good hands" (p.68) — and this is one of them.

principles.name: Call a tight raise with the calling list

feedback.correct: On the list against a strong range: call. Against a tight raiser you reraise only aces, kings and A5s, and call with "the other pocket pairs, any two suited cards ten or higher, the suited connectors, and ace-king offsuit" (p.61).
feedback.too_loose: Calling tight raises with marginal hands burns money.
feedback.too_tight: This hand is on the calling list against a strong range. Folding everything is not the same as avoiding strength.
feedback.too_aggressive: Reraising into a range of aces, kings and ace-king is attacking strength, which is the one thing this chapter says not to do.

principles.rationale: Tight opponents rarely 3-bet light. pp.63, 65-66, 69-70 extend this beyond early position: "Against a raise you consider strong... you want to respond as you would to a raise from early position" (cutoff), "Against a tight raise, you'll still play roughly as you did from early position" (button), and the same again for the blinds.

principles.name: Attack tight raise from EP (3-Bet)

feedback.correct: "Against a raise we think is strong, we reraise only the strongest hands (and a single bluff hand, A5s)" — aces, kings, and the one bluff (pp.61-62).
feedback.too_passive: Flatting premiums against a tight range surrenders preflop initiative.
feedback.too_tight: Aces and kings do not fold to a tight raiser. Against a narrow range these are the hands that still want the money in.

principles.rationale: A tight opener has a narrow, strong range. You must limit your 3-betting range strictly to ultra-premiums that can compete against it. pp.63, 65-66, 69-70 extend this beyond early position: "Against a raise you consider strong... you want to respond as you would to a raise from early position" (cutoff), "Against a tight raise, you'll still play roughly as you did from early position" (button), and the same again for the blinds.

principles.name: Attack loose raise from EP (3-Bet)

feedback.correct: "Against a raise that represents too loose a range of hands, we reraise more": "QQ, AK (suited and offsuit), all the suited aces A5s-A2s, and T9s and 87s" (p.61).
feedback.too_passive: Flat calling premiums loses equity.
feedback.too_tight: A loose raiser is the reason to reraise, not a reason to fold. "When our opponents are playing too many hands, we attack them with bets and raises."

principles.rationale: "When our opponents are playing too many hands, we attack them with bets and raises with both good and bad hands. When our opponents have strong, narrow ranges, we back off. Against a raise we think is strong, we reraise only the strongest hands (and a single bluff hand, A5s). Against a raise that represents too loose a range of hands, we reraise more." (p.62) "You still must be careful, though, since when you're in early position, you have at least four players to act behind you who may turn up with a monster hand."

principles.name: Defend loose raise from EP (Call)

feedback.correct: On the flat-calling list against a loose early raise — "JJ-22, AQs-A6s, KTs+, QTs+, JTs, 98s, 76s, AQo" (p.62). The reraising list is a different, shorter one.
feedback.too_loose: Defending trash out of position burns money.
feedback.too_tight: This hand is on the flat-calling list against a loose raiser. Folding it concedes to the exact opponent you make money from.
feedback.too_aggressive: Reraising this widens the pot with a hand the passage keeps for calling. The reraising list is a different, shorter list.

principles.rationale: The book names the hands that reraise a loose raise and the hands that call it. "These ranges are tighter than button ranges when you're not up against a raise, since even a loose raiser is typically stronger than a limper or two. Raising ranges — even loose ones — typically include the monster hands like A-A and K-K, while limping ranges often exclude these hands." (p.65)

feedback.too_tight: On the calling list against a loose raise. Folding here is playing tighter than the book, not smarter than it.
feedback.too_aggressive: Kept for calling rather than reraising, so the pot stays a size this hand can play after the flop.

feedback.correct: From the button "the emphasis in the 3-betting ranges ... has shifted from premium hands and bluffs (i.e., A-A, K-K, and A-5 suited) to premium hands and other strong hands" — fewer players left to wake up with a monster, "and also because you're assured position in the pot" (pp.66-67).

feedback.too_tight: From the button against a loose raiser, this reraises. Position plus a weak range is the whole argument for it.

feedback.correct: On the button's flat-calling list. "These ranges are tighter than button ranges when you're not up against a raise, since even a loose raiser is typically stronger than a limper or two" (p.66) — wide, and not unlimited.
feedback.too_loose: Do not expand calling range too wide.
feedback.too_tight: A button calling range against a loose raise is wide. Folding this plays a fraction of the hands the seat can profitably see a flop with.
feedback.too_aggressive: This one calls. The button reraising list shifts toward premium hands, "since even a loose raiser is typically stronger than a limper".

principles.name: Attack weak steals

feedback.correct: "Steal raises are made with weak, wide ranges. Therefore, they should be attacked. You should be much more inclined to reraise a potential steal raise than any other type of pre-flop raise from any other position" (p.71).
feedback.too_passive: Failing to 3-bet allows cheap equity realization.
feedback.too_tight: "Steal raises are made with weak, wide ranges. Therefore, they should be attacked." Folding hands off this list is exactly what the stealer is counting on.
feedback.wrong_sizing: A large reraise. "I would make it $35 to go" over a $12 steal — big enough that a hand like eight-five suited pays for the privilege.

principles.rationale: "Steal raises are made with weak, wide ranges. Therefore, they should be attacked. You should be much more inclined to reraise a potential steal raise than any other type of pre-flop raise from any other position." (p.71) "The prototypical steal raise is when everyone folds to a button raise ... Also, if one or two players limp, and an aggressive player on the button raises, this raise as well may often be treated as a steal raise." (pp.70-71)

principles.name: Defend steal raise from Blinds (Call)

feedback.correct: "In addition to all the reraising, against a steal raise you can call with lots of hands" (p.72). The blinds defend "36 percent of the time against a steal-raise", and more of that is calling than reraising (p.73).
feedback.too_loose: Defending trash creates disasters.
feedback.too_tight: You defend 36 percent against a steal. Folding this is treating a wide, weak range as if it were a strong one.
feedback.too_aggressive: This hand defends by calling. The reraising list against a steal is separate and does not include it.

principles.rationale: "In addition to all the reraising, against a steal raise you can call with lots of hands." (p.72) Steal raises "are made with weak, wide ranges" (p.71), and the book lists the hands that call one.

principles.name: Fold to late aggression

feedback.correct: Players rarely bluff enough on late streets: fold what can only beat a bluff, and call only with the combination draw.
feedback.too_loose: "Simply put, don't pay people off." Small-stakes players rarely bluff for big money on the turn or river; when you can only beat a bluff, you fold — top pair, even two pair once the straights and flushes are out there.
feedback.too_tight: A combination draw is the hand this chapter makes room for. It has too much equity against a big turn or river bet to be thrown away with the rest.
feedback.too_aggressive: Against a big bet "I would not bluff, since there's an excellent chance your opponent will simply go with his hand" (p.199). The combination draw calls; nothing here raises.

principles.rationale: Large turn and river bets are heavily weighted toward value. No-pair hands are the clearest case of all: "If you call, you win only if your opponent is bluffing" (p.83) — you can only beat a bluff, so you fold. At 2-5 the big bet is a bet-sizing tell as well: "Say your opponent bets $140. This is the \"big\" bet. Your opponent is betting out because he has a strong hand ... I'd expect to see at least two pair from this opponent" (p.195); "Against this bet size, I would not bluff, since there's an excellent chance your opponent will simply go with his hand" (p.199).

feedback.correct: "Naturally, having outs is a good reason to call a large turn bet, even if you can't beat the hand your opponent is representing" (p.87). The combination draw has too much equity to be thrown away with the rest.

principles.name: Call turn with outs

feedback.correct: "Yes, your opponent is representing a hand that beats you (a flush or straight). But you have ten outs to beat those hands ... you have way too much chance to win to fold to just a $70 bet in a $119 pot" (pp.86-87).
feedback.too_tight: Folding strong draws surrenders equity.
feedback.too_aggressive: Raising turns a hand with ten outs into a bluff and folds out everything you beat. The outs are a reason to see the river cheaply, not to build the pot.

principles.rationale: "You should call. Yes, your opponent is representing a hand that beats you (a flush or straight). But you have ten outs to beat those hands... you have way too much chance to win to fold to just a $70 bet in a $119 pot" (pp.86-87). The outs are the set's redraws to a full house, so the hand class alone carries the claim.

principles.name: Fold river after turn call

feedback.correct: "By the river, most of the ways to win had evaporated ... your opponent committed a final time to playing his hand for stacks." And "never feel like you have to call the river because you called the turn" (p.87).
feedback.right_idea_wrong_spot: Treat previous street calls as sunk costs.
feedback.too_loose: "You are never committed to calling a bet on the end." Calling the turn bought a card, not an obligation.

principles.rationale: River shoves polarize ranges to the nuts. The fold list includes a set because the book's own example does: "say you make the call, the river bricks, and your opponent shoves all-in. Now you should probably fold" -- holding bottom set (pp.86-87).

principles.name: Value bet to be called

feedback.correct: "When you flop a hand like top pair or two pair, your goal should be to bet your hand such that your opponents with weaker hands will pay the maximum to lose at showdown" (p.97).
feedback.too_aggressive: Betting too big specifically to force folds wastes value.
feedback.too_passive: Giving a free card when you are ahead always costs something, and always checking your two-street hands forks your range — "When you flop a value hand, you do not want to push everyone out of the pot", but you do want to get paid (pp.94-104).
feedback.wrong_sizing: A size worse hands still call. Betting too big turns a value hand into a bluff and folds out everyone you beat.

principles.rationale: "What value does a good hand have in poker? Just this: when you get to showdown, you turn the hand over. If no one can beat your hand, you win the pot. That's it. That's the sole value of a good hand. It comes only at showdown." (p.93) "When you hold a hand with real showdown value, you don't want everyone to fold. You want to take the hand to showdown, and you want your opponents to pay you along the way." (p.95) "When you flop a hand like top pair or two pair, your goal should be to bet your hand such that your opponents with weaker hands will pay the maximum to lose at showdown." (p.97)

principles.name: Bet a value hand early on a draw-heavy board

feedback.correct: "When the board allows for a number of draws, it is usually best to bet earlier in the hand ... draws are most likely to call the flop, less likely to call the turn, and they will not call at all on the river" (p.103).
feedback.too_passive: Checking a value hand here gives the free card to exactly the hands that would have paid you on the flop.

principles.rationale: "When the board allows for a number of draws, it is usually best to bet earlier in the hand for two reasons. One, draws are most likely to call the flop, less likely to call the turn, and they will not call at all on the river... Two, when you bet draw-heavy boards, your opponents have to determine whether you are betting a made hand or a draw" (p.103).

principles.name: No slowplaying monsters

feedback.correct: "When you slowplay, you forfeit the chance to get three streets of value — and that third street is by far the most valuable street in hold 'em" (p.106). "When you flop a monster, your goal is to stack your opponent. That process starts with a bet" (p.107).
feedback.too_passive: Checking back forfeits future river bets.
feedback.wrong_sizing: "Bet big enough with big hands so you can comfortably bet all-in by the river." A small suck-them-in bet starts a plan that cannot finish.

principles.rationale: "Slowplaying. Don't. Especially at the 1-2 level ... By \"slowplaying\" I mean specifically checking back a hand on the flop that potentially has three streets of value ... When you slowplay, you forfeit the chance to get three streets of value — and that third street is by far the most valuable street in hold 'em, since the pot has grown and the bets are the biggest." (p.106)

principles.name: Bet sizing for stacks

feedback.correct: Geometrical betting makes calling down easier.
feedback.wrong_sizing: Small flop bets require impossible river overbets.
feedback.too_passive: Checking a monster gives a free card and starts the plan a street late: "You do not want to start that plan off with a free card."

principles.rationale: "Bet big enough with big hands so you can comfortably bet all-in by the river. This is an extension of the \"don't slowplay three-street hands\" concept ... If you flop a set, for example, your goal is to try to win stacks. You don't want to start that plan off with a free card. You don't want to start it off with a small \"suck them in\" bet either ... It's generally easier to get a pot-sized bet or larger called on the flop than the river. So you want to build the pot early and give your opponent something more callable on the river." (pp.109-110)

principles.name: Relentless value loose games

feedback.correct: "When you have trouble winning in loose games with lots of calling stations, it's often due to one problem: you don't bet your hands enough" (p.114). "When you flop top pair or better, you bet. You keep betting until someone raises you" (p.117).
feedback.too_passive: Checking down out of fear leaves money on the table.
feedback.wrong_sizing: Bet big. In loose games "many hands are worth three streets of value" — $12 into $12, $50 into $60 — and with less than a pot behind the bet is the stack: "There's $136 left in your stack, and there's $210 in the pot. Shove."

principles.rationale: "When you have trouble winning in loose games with lots of calling stations, it's often due to one problem: you don't bet your hands enough ... many hands are worth three streets of value in these games." Bet the flop, bet the turn, and shove the river — "If this really is a game where no one folds to bluffs, they won't fold here either" (pp.114-116).

principles.name: Cbet opponent range

feedback.correct: C-bet into a wide pre-flop range that mostly missed — except the very wet flop your hand does not touch, which you concede.
feedback.too_passive: On a flop that missed their range, "when they check, you bet" — "it's far more important to C-bet on the 8-4-2 flop than on the K-4-2 flop. I would nearly always C-bet the 8-4-2 flop" (p.152). Checking hands your opponent folds to is giving up the automatic profit.
feedback.too_aggressive: Not this flop with this hand. "On very wet boards like T♣9♠7♣, concede the pot if you hold a hand like A♦4♦ that doesn't connect in any way" — restrict bluff barrels to hands with a piece of the board (p.178).
feedback.wrong_sizing: A c-bet is about what your OPPONENT holds, not what you represent — half to three-quarters pot does the work without pricing you in.

principles.rationale: "The bet's success or failure has everything to do with what other players hold, and little or nothing to do with what the bettor holds (or what he represents holding) ... If someone has a king, they're calling. If someone doesn't have a king, on a board like K-4-2 rainbow, if you bet big enough there's a good chance they're folding." (pp.151-152) "Barreling is not about what you hold or what you could hold." (p.152) "In a typical 2-5 game, it's far more important to C-bet on the 8-4-2 flop than on the K-4-2 flop. In fact, on the king-high flop, I might even check it back with the intention of betting the turn if everyone again checks to me. I would nearly always C-bet, however, the 8-4-2 flop." (p.152)

feedback.correct: On a high, dry flop the C-bet is fine and so is the check: "on the king-high flop, I might even check it back with the intention of betting the turn if everyone again checks to me" (p.152).
A C-bet is about what THEY hold: "if people fold, it's not out of fear that the pre-flop raiser hit a king. They fold because they likely missed the flop" (p.151). Their wide range missed; bet.
"On very wet boards like T♣9♠7♣, concede the pot if you hold a hand like A♦4♦ that doesn't connect in any way" (p.178). So many hands with real equity connect here that a naked barrel burns money.

exceptions.note: p.178: on very wet boards, concede the pot with a hand that does not connect in any way.

principles.name: Barrel the turn after your flop bet was called

feedback.correct: "When they check to you on the turn, and you won't be able to win a showdown without improvement, bet. Your turn bet is rarely a bad bet. It's frequently enormously profitable" (p.154).
feedback.too_passive: "Bet, and don't be shy about it." The flop call told you they have something; the brick turn told you it did not improve — "most of the time they will fold" to a nice-sized bet (pp.154-155).
feedback.wrong_sizing: A real turn bet. With stacks behind, "bet $100" into $120 and "$120" into $162 (p.155); with smaller stacks "I'd pare down the size of my turn bet to perhaps $140" into $222 (p.238). Not a small one, and not the stack.

principles.rationale: "Above all, remember this about barreling: when they check to you on the turn, and you won't be able to win a showdown without improvement, bet. Your turn bet is rarely a bad bet. It's frequently enormously profitable. If you aren't good at figuring out when to bet, you're much better off betting all your weak hands than betting none of them." (p.154)

principles.name: Barrel the turn when the raiser checks to you

feedback.correct: "The turn is the 6♣. The raiser checks. Bet, and don't be shy about it" (p.155). His flop bet was the automatic one; the check says the turn did not help him.
feedback.too_passive: "The raiser checks. Bet, and don't be shy about it." His flop bet was the automatic one; the check says the turn did not help him, and "most of the time they will fold" to a real bet (pp.154-155).
feedback.wrong_sizing: A real turn bet. With stacks behind, "bet $100" into $120 and "$120" into $162 (p.155); with smaller stacks "I'd pare down the size of my turn bet to perhaps $140" into $222 (p.238). Not a small one, and not the stack.

principles.rationale: "Say you have J♦T♦. Your opponent opens for $20, someone calls, and you call on the button ... The pre-flop raiser bets $30 ... you call with your open-ended straight draw. The turn is the 6♣. The raiser checks. Bet, and don't be shy about it." (pp.154-155) The same rule as barrelling your own c-bet: "when they check to you on the turn, and you won't be able to win a showdown without improvement, bet."

principles.name: C-bet multiway with real equity and money behind

feedback.correct: "Your bet thins the field ... sets up betting on future rounds and keeps the nuts in your range ... It builds a pot worth stealing, and takes advantage of even loose players' tendencies to get skittish when playing enormous pots" (p.160).
feedback.too_passive: Checking denies you the sets in your story and lets someone spike a free card.

principles.rationale: "Don't C-bet flops you miss into four or more opponents unless there's money behind and you have significant equity-when-called" (p.159). With $1,000 stacks — "the stack-to-pot ratio is about 8. With the higher stack-to-pot ratio, you'll be able to fire multiple barrels" — and a gutshot, two overcards and a backdoor nut flush draw on J-T-3, the same author bets (p.160): the bet thins the field, keeps the nuts in your range, builds a pot worth stealing, and invites the raise that warns you off.

principles.name: Bet twice on a somewhat wet board when the turn bricks

feedback.correct: "A large number of hands has hit this flop, very few hands have hit it hard. Nearly all of these hands will feel like they need to improve on the turn" — and a brick improved none of them.
feedback.too_passive: On these boards "you shouldn't even consider betting just once and giving up ... if you fire that one bluff and give up when called, you'll burn through money."
feedback.wrong_sizing: A nice-sized turn bet. On a board where "very few hands have hit it hard", the size is what makes marginal hands give up.

principles.rationale: "On somewhat wet boards like Q-9-6, you shouldn't even consider betting just once and giving up. You're so likely to have your first bet called ... But these are terrific boards on which to bet twice. You bet the flop, fully expecting to get called. Then you avoid a danger card like a jack, ten, or eight on the turn. If the turn card bricks for this flop, you bluff a nice amount and win more than your share of these kinds of pots." (p.178) Scoped to `gapped` alone (2026-09-13): the rule also required `straight_possible`, which no board like Q-9-6 carries — a made straight there needs three more ranks — so it could not match the board its own page names. With connectedness now decided by whether two hole cards make an open-ender, Q-9-6 is gapped, which is the class the passage is about.

principles.name: Abandon very wet air

feedback.correct: "On very wet boards like T♣9♠7♣, concede the pot if you hold a hand like A♦4♦ that doesn't connect in any way. So many hands with real equity connect with this board, you should restrict your bluff barrels to those times you hold a hand that also has a piece of the board" (p.178).
feedback.too_aggressive: Bluffing air into combo boards burns money.

principles.rationale: "On very wet boards like T♣9♠7♣, concede the pot if you hold a hand like A♦4♦ that doesn't connect in any way. So many hands with real equity connect with this board, you should restrict your bluff barrels to those times you hold a hand that also has a piece of the board." (p.178)

principles.name: Attack a monochrome flop

feedback.correct: "It's hard to make a flush" — 45 flushes out of some 600 hands — and "many players have an outsized fear of them because a flush is an obvious threat."
feedback.too_passive: "Although flushes are hard to flop, many players have an outsized fear of them." Checking concedes a pot that fear would have handed you.
feedback.too_aggressive: Bet, do not jam. Monochrome boards are profitable to attack precisely because a normal bet is enough to fold out non-flushes.

principles.rationale: "This player playing any two suited cards will flop a flush on a three-flush board just 7.5 percent of the time. That's not that scary, is it? ... This misunderstanding about the frequency of flopped flushes often means you can aggressively play monochrome boards to steal more than your share of pots." (p.181) The math is stated about one opponent; the multiway monochrome flop is p.186's ("a flop like 8♣4♣2♣ can be a great one to barrel in multi-way pots").

principles.name: Check-raise the limper who bets the ace-high flop

feedback.correct: "The button's limping range performs poorly on most flops that contain an ace ... There's a good chance the bet is weak, and you should check-raise (or check-call, and plan to bet a later street) with impunity."
feedback.too_tight: Folding to a bet his range cannot back is paying impunity forward.

principles.rationale: "Aggressive players will usually raise the button after limpers, who typically limp low-card hands... It would be odd for an aggressive player to limp the button with a hand that contains an ace. Therefore, the button's limping range performs poorly on most flops that contain an ace... There is a good chance the bet is weak, and you should check-raise (or check-call, and plan to bet a later street) with impunity." The read is about HIS range, but the hands the argument is FOR are the ones with little or no showdown value — Miller's own hand here is Q-Q on A-9-6 (skill5_ex3, an underpair). Top pair and better need no impunity and this passage does not discuss them, so they abstain rather than being claimed by silence.

principles.name: Give up ace-high flops against a loose field

feedback.correct: "Aces make up a significant percentage of many people's pre-flop ranges. So it's unlikely four or five players will all fail to have one."
feedback.too_aggressive: With one opponent "you probably should bet, hoping your opponent doesn't have an ace and folds" — against four or five, someone has it, and you "have relatively little equity-when-called".

principles.rationale: "Ace-high flops can be fine to C-bet into one or two opponents, but are often a pass against four or five loose players ... Because you're likely to get called by an ace, and you have relatively little equity-when-called in this situation, give up." (pp.185-186)

principles.name: Call the flop to read the turn sizing

feedback.correct: "By flat-calling the flop and waiting for your opponent to act on the turn, you allow him to give you information that's potentially useful" (p.200). And when the bet is small into two opponents, "the bet size belies that story a bit ... You can call and see what he does on the turn" (pp.238-239).
feedback.too_aggressive: "If you raise here, and your opponent does want to play, you could be up against a strong set of hands against which your hand doesn't have the equity it looks like it should have." Call, and read his turn bet.
feedback.too_tight: This is "a hand this strong and flexible" — the nut flush draw and a pair. Folding it to a half-pot C-bet gives up the hand and the read.

principles.rationale: "Many players are tempted to turn this hand immediately into a bluff ... I think this is a suboptimal use of a hand this strong and flexible. Right now you don't have a lot of information about what the pre-flop raiser has ... Potentially, your hand performs better when you allow your opponent to give you information when he bets his strong hands on the turn. You do this by flat-calling the flop, seeing a turn card, and then looking for a bet-sizing tell." (pp.198-199)

principles.name: Raise the small turn probe into your c-bet

feedback.correct: "Raise. All day long." The small bet is "an attempt to see where he's at ... His plan is to fold if you raise."
feedback.too_passive: Calling lets him see where he is at for the price he chose. "So make him fold."
feedback.too_tight: "His plan is to fold if you raise. So make him fold." A small out-of-flow bet is the invitation, not the danger.
feedback.wrong_sizing: "You can just blow him out of the water by raising his $60 bet to $180 or more. Or, if you want to get greedy ... you can min-raise him to $120." Either; not a shove.

principles.rationale: "You bet $40, and the big blind calls. The turn is the T♠. Your opponent now bets $60 into the $142 pot ... Raise. All day long. The player in the big blind has an ace with a kicker he's worried about. He check-calls the flop, and then he bets out on the non-club turn card in an attempt to see where he's at ... So he bets around half-pot. His plan is to fold if you raise. That's the entire point of keeping the bet on the small side — so he saves money if he has to fold. So make him fold." (p.241) The small turn bet forks his range into "marginal hands the player will likely be willing to fold" (p.196).

principles.name: Bluff-raise the raiser's small turn bet

feedback.correct: "Against a bet of this size, I would bluff-raise" — the $50 or $60 turn bet is the marginal part of his range, "hands that ... aren't strong enough to play for stacks" (p.199).
feedback.too_passive: Calling lets a hand that is not strong enough to play for stacks keep the lead for the price it chose. The small bet is the part of his range to attack.
feedback.too_tight: Folding to the small turn bet gives up on exactly the hands p.199 says to bluff — the weak king, the pair-plus-draw, the lesser flush draw. "If he bets $90 or more" is the fold; this is not that bet.
feedback.wrong_sizing: A real raise. The point is to move a hand that "isn't strong enough to play for stacks" off the pot; a min-raise invites the call and a shove risks the stack against the part of his range you cannot beat.

principles.rationale: "Say on this K♥T♥7♦8♣ board your opponent bets just $50 or $60. This bet could be a number of things. It could be a weak king like K♣5♣. It could be a pair-plus-draw hand, like J-T or 9-8. It could be a flush draw weaker than yours. Against a bet of this size, I would bluff-raise. Many of the hands players put in this $50 or $60 turn-bet range are exactly the hands against which you should be trying to bluff. These are hands that have your pair of sevens beaten but aren't strong enough to play for stacks." (p.199)

principles.name: Consistent own sizing

feedback.correct: n/a — not drillable.

principles.rationale: Varying bet sizing based strictly on absolute hand strength allows observant opponents to perfectly map your range.

principles.name: Profile based 4betting

feedback.correct: Old-school 3-bettors only reraise premiums.
feedback.too_aggressive: 4-bet bluffing against this profile wastes chips.

principles.rationale: A 3-bet from an old-school profile is exclusively premium hands.

principles.name: Emotional numbing

feedback.correct: n/a — not drillable.

principles.rationale: Bankroll management and emotional discipline are vital but not drillable.

principles.name: The Pitfalls of Running Good

feedback.correct: n/a — concept rule

principles.rationale: Running good can instill bad habits. Avoid entering unprofitable pots loosely, attacking strong players unnecessarily, attempting bad bluffs due to overconfidence, or overusing 'pet plays' like double check-raises.

principles.name: The Pitfalls of Running Bad

feedback.correct: n/a — concept rule

principles.rationale: Running bad can erode core skills. Avoid losing your aggression, making hopeless calls to 'see it anyway', preferring all-in plays early in hands out of frustration, or failing to cut sessions short to protect your bankroll.

principles.name: Attack bloated frequencies

feedback.correct: "Of course he bet there" is the tell: "there's an excellent chance he's bluffing too many hands for what his hand range can support" (p.261). "When you have the range strength advantage in a pot, it is your right to continue with some weak hands hidden among all the strong ones" (p.260).
feedback.too_tight: Folding allows them to bluff away junk hands.

principles.rationale: He raised a wide range and you called a tighter one, so your range is the stronger — yet he C-bets almost every flop "because he raised". A predictable bet from a weaker range is an exploitable bet: "you can call with nothing", or raise, hidden among the strong hands you also hold (pp.258-261).

principles.name: Fold to a LAG's big third barrel

feedback.correct: "You should fold to this bet, as a big river bet is often the marker that the LAG actually has a hand" — "while the $80 flop bet and the $200 turn bet are reliable from this player, the $660 on the river is a rarity" (pp.262-263).
feedback.too_loose: Calling attempts to pick off a statistically non-existent bluff.

principles.rationale: "Many players are willing to fire one or two shots, but usually give up if you refuse to go away. This is, indeed, the principle tactic employed by classic loose-aggressive players (LAGs) ... some players are so predictable in this style of play you can actually use Skill #2 against them, meaning don't pay them off if there's a third barrel ... You should fold to this bet, as a big river bet is often the marker that the LAG actually has a hand ... while the $80 flop bet and the $200 turn bet are reliable from this player, the $660 on the river is a rarity." (pp.262-263)

principles.name: Call last ditch bluff

feedback.correct: The turn check-back is what a strong hand would not do — "most players with strong hands would bet to get calls from weaker hands, and to charge the draws" — so "instead of giving up on the pot, he's making a last-ditch bluff attempt" (p.264).
feedback.too_tight: Folding ignores the context of their prior weak action.
feedback.too_aggressive: Raising folds out the busted draw you are trying to catch. "Instead of giving up on the pot, he is making a last-ditch bluff attempt" — let him.

principles.rationale: The turn check-back is what a strong hand would not do — "most players with strong hands would bet to get calls from weaker hands, and to charge the draws" — so the river raise is unsupported by his range. At 1-2 that raise is rare enough to fold to; at 5-10, against a player this aggressive, "I would consider calling, even if my hand is guaranteed to lose" to a value hand (p.264).

principles.name: Call a 3-bet deep, in position

feedback.correct: "You should probably call the reraise. You don't want to get pushed off your hands in position, or else you'll be playing too many of your hands from out of position" (p.272).
feedback.too_tight: Folding every 3-bet when deep means playing your whole range out of position.
feedback.too_aggressive: A 4-bet turns a positional edge into a coin flip for a huge pot.

principles.rationale: "You should probably call the reraise. You do not want to get pushed off your hands in position, or else you will be playing too many of your hands from out of position." The extra stack depth is what pays for the call — the same facing state at 1/2 with normal stacks is a fold (Skill #2, pp.88-89).

principles.name: Fold the good-but-not-great hand to a deep all-in

feedback.correct: "You should be considerably tighter with the set of hands you're willing to get all-in. It only makes sense you should be choosier with hands you play for $6,000 than those you play for $2,000" (p.270).
feedback.too_loose: Committing deep stacks with marginals is devastating.

principles.rationale: "You should be considerably tighter with the set of hands you're willing to get all-in. It only makes sense you should be choosier with hands you play for $6,000 than those you play for $2,000." (p.270) The hands a normal stack would call off with — top pair, an overpair, two pair on a board that has moved — are the ones that extra bet is choosier about.

principles.name: Reverse live reads

feedback.correct: n/a — not drillable.

principles.rationale: Observant professionals punish weak betting lines aggressively. Relying on reversing live reads is contextual to physical tells.

principles.name: Finding a pro's leaks in a turn bet

feedback.correct: n/a — concept rule

principles.rationale: A pro who checks the turn is usually pot-controlling a one-or-two-street hand; a big turn bet is either an extra-strong hand or a bluff, and "the question is, what percentage of the time is he bluffing?" Three puzzle pieces: board texture ("if a given board allows fewer strong hands, it's likely the pro could be over-bluffing"), his pre-flop hand selection (a K-9-7-3 board holds more of his strong hands than K-7-6-3), and his overall skew toward bluffing or showdowns. "Consider all these factors then examine the turn bet."

principles.name: Gto study

feedback.correct: n/a — not drillable.

principles.rationale: GTO play is theoretical, and the decisions it changes are not the ones this book is teaching you to make at a live table.

principles.name: Fold to a 3-bet from someone who never 3-bets

feedback.correct: "When you raise pre-flop, and you get 3-bet by an opponent who rarely makes this play, you should usually fold ... with normal-sized stacks, you're usually better off folding the hands like 66 and QJs and the like that can't reasonably compete with a range of super-premium hands" (pp.88-89).
feedback.too_loose: Calling a 3-bet with a hand that cannot compete with aces, kings and ace-king is how stacks go. "When you raise pre-flop, and you get 3-bet by an opponent who rarely makes this play, you should usually fold."

principles.rationale: At these stakes a 3-bet is a narrow range of premium hands. "With normal-sized stacks, you're usually better off folding the hands like 66 and QJs and the like that can't reasonably compete with a range of super-premium hands." The in_range side is omitted deliberately: p.88 says these players 3-bet "very strong hands like aces, kings, and ace-king", and the book never states the line for holding aces yourself here -- an omitted side abstains rather than guesses.

principles.name: Call a big turn raise holding a set

feedback.correct: "Maybe you can beat some of the hands your opponent is representing, but not others ... if you can list more than a few hands you can beat, it's often a call" (p.88) — and the set is still drawing to a full house.
feedback.too_tight: Folding a set that beats several represented hands is over-applying Skill #2.
feedback.too_aggressive: Calling is enough with relatively little left behind. Reraising ends the hand against exactly the hands that beat you.

principles.rationale: Skill #2 does not apply when you beat part of the range and can still draw out: "you can beat some of the hands your opponent is representing... you also can draw out on the straight, the main hand you're worried about."

principles.name: Commit an overpair to a flop check-raise

feedback.correct: "You need to win only a little more than 35 percent of the time to justify a call ... you should move all-in since there's relatively little money left after you call your opponent's raise" — "when your opponent forces the issue on flops like this — especially when the pot was 3-bet pre-flop — and you have an overpair, often you just have to gamble" (p.139).
feedback.too_tight: Folding an overpair here gives up on the pot odds the 3-bet built.
feedback.too_passive: Flat-calling leaves a stack behind and a river you cannot play. "You should move all-in since there is relatively little money left."
feedback.wrong_sizing: All in. With relatively little left behind after calling the raise, anything smaller commits you without the fold equity.

principles.rationale: "when your opponent forces the issue on flops like this—especially when the pot was 3-bet pre-flop—and you have an overpair, often you just have to gamble." Skill #2 is about the TURN and RIVER; this is a big FLOP bet, where the pot odds carry it.

principles.name: Give up the river on a static board

feedback.correct: "If your bluffs haven't worked after betting the flop and turn on a static board, there's a good chance you should give up" (p.171). "By the time the turn is bet and called, the caller will have a small remaining set of fairly strong hands. Barreling time, for this pot at least, is over" (p.173).
feedback.too_aggressive: A third barrel here asks them to fold a hand they already like.

principles.rationale: "if your bluffs haven't worked after betting the flop and turn on a static board, there's a good chance you should give up." The caller's confidence has not moved; a third barrel is a pure power play against a hand they like.

principles.name: Fire the river when a dynamic board bricks

feedback.correct: The caller on a dynamic board "could hold anything from a pair to a flush draw to a straight draw", and the river card "is likely a bad card for the caller almost no matter what hand he holds".
feedback.too_passive: "Because the flop started out dynamic, your opponent will likely have found more hands to call with on the flop and turn. But by the river, a significant percentage of these hands will have bricked out."
feedback.wrong_sizing: A final barrel "of perhaps $300 into the $522 pot" — a bit over half. By the river "a significant percentage of these hands will have bricked out", and this is the size that asks them.

principles.rationale: "if your bluff bets haven't worked on a dynamic board, you may still want to give a river bluff a shot. It's likely your opponents are still drawing and by the river, have missed everything."

principles.name: Barrel the turn on two wheel cards

feedback.correct: "Since many players play any ace, these gutshot draws are fairly common on two wheel-card flops. As long as a third wheel card doesn't hit the turn, you should probably barrel" (p.179).
feedback.too_passive: Checking lets every ace-x gutshot see a free river.

principles.rationale: "boards whose flops have two non-ace wheel cards will generally see more calls—and more folds on the turn... Since many players play any ace, these gutshot draws are fairly common. As long as a third wheel card doesn't hit the turn, you should probably barrel."

principles.name: Attack a paired low flop that checks through

feedback.correct: "It's hard for anyone to make a good hand on this flop ... As the pre-flop raiser, you can represent A-A and often get anyone not holding at least a deuce to fold." Bet small: "if I actually held A-A, I'd probably bet that much", "it lets you off cheap if someone check-raises", and "it encourages people to call with marginal hands" (pp.249-250).
feedback.too_passive: Checking gives up a pot almost nobody connected with.
feedback.wrong_sizing: Small. "I would bet on the small side like $40 or $50" — it looks like the aces you are representing, and it lets you off cheap if raised.

principles.rationale: "It's hard for anyone to make a good hand on this flop... you want flops where it's difficult to make anything at all. As the pre-flop raiser, you can represent A-A and often get anyone not holding at least a deuce to fold." Connected boards are excluded: the whole argument is that "it is hard for anyone to make a good hand on this flop" (p.249), which stops being true the moment the board offers straight draws — and pp.177-178 say to concede those rather than barrel them.

principles.name: Barrel the turn with a small pair as a bluff

feedback.correct: "This hand has zero streets of value ... Often, it's more accurate to treat hands like this where you pair a smaller board card as bluffing hands. You can get people to fold stronger hands, and if you're called by top pair, you have five outs" (p.239).
feedback.too_passive: Checking gives up the fold equity that is the only value this hand has.
feedback.wrong_sizing: About half the pot. "I would bet about $70 into the $127 pot. The bet is big enough to get your opponent to release most of your targeted hands."

principles.rationale: "Often, it's more accurate to treat hands like this where you pair a smaller board card as bluffing hands. You can get people to fold stronger hands, and if you're called by top pair, you have five outs ... In this case, I would treat the hand as a bluff, because there's a good chance your opponent has a hand like A-Q or T-T, and there's also a good chance he'll fold these hands to pressure." (pp.239-240) "This hand falls under the \"when in doubt, bet the turn,\" line of thinking."

principles.name: Raise the out-of-position C-bet on a dynamic flop

feedback.correct: "There's a good chance your opponent is out of line on a bet. Harness your positional advantage on this dynamic board texture by immediately challenging your opponent."
feedback.too_passive: "Give him a reason not to" fire. Calling lets a raiser who "should be checking a lot" keep barrelling a board that is his to miss.
feedback.too_tight: "You have overcards, a gutshot, and a backdoor flush draw, which is plenty of equity-when-called." This is the hand you challenge with.
feedback.wrong_sizing: "I'd raise to about $90" — three times his bet. Enough that a hand betting out of line has to give up.

principles.rationale: "This is a dynamic flop that your opponent, an out-of-position pre-flop raiser, should be checking a lot. But if this player is like most at 2-5 ... he is going to fire away until given a reason not to. So, give him a reason not to. You have overcards, a gutshot, and a backdoor flush draw, which is plenty of equity-when-called ... Harness your positional advantage on this dynamic board texture by immediately challenging your opponent." (p.246)

principles.name: Min-raise a small out-of-flow probe with an overpair

feedback.correct: "This small, out-of-flow bet (your opponent did not 'check to the raiser') is typically a probe bet ... you can make a small raise — like a min-raise to $30. The raise shows a bit more strength, but most players won't be able to resist calling it" (p.135).
feedback.too_aggressive: A big raise wins the pot instead of the stack, which is the whole loss.
feedback.too_tight: Aces do not fold to a $15 probe bet. "Do not let a bet like this scare you off a big hand."
feedback.wrong_sizing: A min-raise. "If you raise big and fire money at the pot, your opponent will fold. That is the information he is looking for."

principles.rationale: "This small, out-of-flow bet is typically a probe bet... If you raise big and fire money at the pot, your opponent will fold. That is the information he is looking for. Since you do not want this to happen, you should not react this way." A small raise keeps a weak top pair in the pot.

principles.name: Call a small flop bet heads-up with top pair

feedback.correct: "The bet is fairly small, and there are few enough players in the pot that the pre-flop raiser might just be making a standard continuation bet. Your pair of aces could easily be the best hand" (p.90). "Bets on this round are not reliable indicators of strength" (p.85).
feedback.too_tight: Folding top pair to a half-pot c-bet pays off every continuation bet ever made.
feedback.too_aggressive: Raising blows out the weak hands a small flop bet is made with. "Flop bets are not reliable indicators of strength" — so let the weak ones keep betting.

principles.rationale: "The bet is fairly small, and there are few enough players in the pot that the pre-flop raiser might just be making a standard continuation bet. Your pair of aces could easily be the best hand." Skill #2 is about LARGE bets on the turn and river, not this.

principles.name: Fold top pair to a big multiway flop bet
